extracted.intended_audience: apothecaries, herbalists, and practical botanists (readers/practitioners of medicinal-plant preparation)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical instructions and standards for propagating plants, preserving flowers, extracting oils and perfumes, and preparing scented/distilled waters and medicaments from plant materials. Contains propagation modes, preservation/storage rules, apparatus and procedural options for oil/perfume extraction, and guidance on choosing methods to preserve 'virtues'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of plant propagation
rubrics_metrics.description: Plantae propagantur quinqj modis: semine; radice; nodo plantarum; ablaquatione; ac partredine (semine, by root, by nodes/cuttings, by layering/‘ablaquatione’, and by division).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: abies & larix by seed; glycyrrhiza & lilium by root; lilies send forth shoots that root; some plants propagate by tears or lacrymae (Theophrastus' opinion); certain species can propagate by multiple modes (e.g., olea & ficus). Consider the species' natural habit (roots, suckers, nodes) when choosing method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of flowers and fragile plant parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Flowers and delicate plants are preserved when stored in a moist, fatty (viscous) medium and kept in suitable vessels; in chambers flowers can be kept nearly a month.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques: place flowers in warm water or in vessels with fatty viscous liquid; store flowers in rooms (cubiculis) where they remain for a month; selecting a fatty/viscid medium (lenta aqua) retards decay. For long preservation, alternate replacing spent flowers with fresh ones once odor has transferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer cold extraction / avoid coction to preserve virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Optimum oil/substance 'effluit' abfque coctione — the best fragrant/medicinal substance issues forth without coction (without prolonged strong heat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heat- (fire-) extracted substances tend to lose 'pure' virtues; choose maceration/infusion/pressing/distillation methods that avoid overcooking when the aim is to retain delicate odor and medicinal power. If heat is necessary, moderate it and use measures (water/wine) to prevent burning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of extraction methods and expected quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantia olei excipitur totidem modis quot vires ipsae — there are as many ways to extract oil as there are kinds of active virtue; methods differ (cold maceration, heat/coction, distillation, pressing) and yield different qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rank: (1) oils obtained without coction (cold methods) are best; (2) those from gentle processes (maceration, infusion, long sun exposure) are very good; (3) oils extracted by strong fire often lose virtues; (4) distillations yield aromatic waters and concentrated odours but with different characters. Choose method per material and desired property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vessel material and construction matters (use glass where possible)
rubrics_metrics.description: In vitro vas (glass vessel) is better: 'qui quanto latior, eo melior ad vires, odorem, saporem transferendos' — the broader the glass vessel the better for transferring virtues, odour and flavour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer glass (vitreous) vessels and glass canals for distillation and storage of fragrant oils/waters; avoid porous/clay vessels which breathe and diminish transfer. Construct distillation apparatus with pileus (cover), adjoining glass channels and a serpentine canal when feasible to preserve aroma and avoid loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distillation apparatus and procedure for aromatic waters (e.g., rosewater)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distillatio: use a closed vessel (A) covered (pileus), a linen or porous layer (B) to collect, and a collecting plate (C); place over fire so that smoke condenses into water and drips into the receiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange vases and canals so fumes pass into a water-filled receiver; control heat to avoid overcooking; if essential oils are desired in the aqueous distillate, condense fumes by cooling channels; glass tubing and serpentine canals yield better retention of odour. Repeat distillation if a stronger water is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of water or wine as medium/support for extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Aqua (water) and vinum (wine) act as supports or auxiliaries in extracting oils and odours: wine penetrates and dissolves more than water and can aid extraction; water moderates heat and prevents burning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When heating oily substances, add water or wine so the oil does not 'burn' — water/vinegar act as bulking/transfer media. Wine penetrates deeper into materials and can be used where stronger extraction is wanted; water (especially distilled water) is often preferred for aromatic waters. The ratio and choice depend on material and desired character of the extract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for extracting oil from nuts/seeds (seed-specific procedures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different seeds require different extraction methods: e.g., myrtica-type nuts are divided, infused in Cretan wine, dried two days in shade, heated and expressed; other methods include maceration until putrefaction then pressing, or heating and immediate expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose method by seed type and moisture: (a) for copious but milder oil: repeated infusion in Cretan wine and pressing after drying; (b) for richer oil: allow controlled putrefaction in wine then press (do not drink that infusion); (c) for oily kernels (almonds, myristica): purge bark/cortex, heat and press; manage heat carefully as temperature affects yield and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferring floral odor to fats (odorization of oils/lard)
rubrics_metrics.description: To imbue fats with flower odour: lay flowers alternately with oil-bearing substrates (e.g., almonds/myrobalan kernels), compress and keep until the fat absorbs the odour; then replace spent flowers and repeat until maximum scent transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: use amygdala (almonds) or purified myrobalan seeds as carriers; layer flowers and kernels, compress (compreffaque) and keep until floral odour wanes, then remove spent flowers and substitute fresh ones — repeat as needed. Gentle warmth or sun exposure may accelerate transfer; then press or express the scented fat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand humors/moisture-types to predict putrefaction and processing behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Humida quae in mixtis continetur sunt quatuor genera: aquea (watery), mucofa (mucous), pinguia (oily/fatty), imperfecta/mediocriter concocta — each behaves differently in putrefaction and in extraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aqueous humours putrefy quickly; mucous less so; oily (pinguia) are less prone to putrefaction. Extraction, storage and heat-treatment should be chosen according to the humour-type of the plant material: wet/aquatic materials need quicker processing and more careful preservation; oily materials tolerate more handling and give more stable oils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use gentle sun or moderate heat as a preparatory aid (but avoid excessive fire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gentle exposure to sun or moderate heat assists odour absorption and expression (flowers exposed on sun then expressed), but strong fire consumes oil and reduces potency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing oils or infusions, allow sun-drying or mild heating to help release scents; do not subject to prolonged or intense fire. If heat is used, moderate it with water or wine to avoid destruction of volatile compounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storage and ageing effects on liquids (wines, oils, scented waters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cool places preserve wines and certain aromatic qualities; ageing modifies colour and odour (e.g., some wines become whiter with age; percolation through certain stones preserves or alters properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Store in cool locales to retard spoilage; use marble/percolation through Indicus stone to affect colour/odour positively; properly conditioned vessels and cool storage extend life and retain fragrance. Repeated distillation can concentrate or alter qualities of waters.
